Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 25 Aug 2000 10:28:29 GMT, francoi...@my-deja.com wrote:

>I' d like to know if first strike acts before any other normal strike,
>so it can cancel the effect of a Stike: Combat End card.

It cannot. Dodge cancels the opposing minion's initial strike, even
if it were used with First Strike. And S:CE resolves before any other
effects during strike resolution.

>For example, if one of my Assamite enters combat with a Toreador, and
>he plays a Silence of Death (superior level) and a Taste of Death, can
>the Toreador plays a Majesty and avoid going to torpor?

First, by card text, your Taste of Death strike is simply a normal
strike, not with First Strike. (Silence of Death only applies to hand
and melee weapon strikes.)

Second, yes, the Majesty resolves first during strike resolution, and
combat ends immediately. Your strike does not resolve.

-- Derek
Jack-Booted Thug of Atlanta

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
francoi...@my-deja.com wrote:
>
> I' d like to know if first strike acts before any other normal strike,
> so it can cancel the effect of a Stike: Combat End card.

According to the rules, Strike: Combat Ends will "beat" a First Strike,
and a Strike: Dodge will still allow the dodger to avoid the effects of
the First Strike.

> For example, if one of my Assamite enters combat with a Toreador, and
> he plays a Silence of Death (superior level) and a Taste of Death, can
> the Toreador plays a Majesty and avoid going to torpor?

Yes. Note that in your example, the Assamite's strike is just a "normal"
Taste of Death. Silence of Death gives First Strike to only "hand and
melee weapon" strikes. Taste of Death is neither a hand strike nor a
melee weapon strike. (But, even if the Assamite had blocked the
Toreador and played Backstab, the Majesty would still end the combat
before the Taste of Death with First Strike could resolve.)

--

ELDB Dave <eldb...@my-deja.com> wrote:
> In fact, if anyone out there has used this kind of house-rule [First
> Strikes beat Dodge], could you let us know how it went?

My old group (haven't started playing again since moving) played where
First Strikes beat Dodge and Strike: Combat Ends.

We didn't use equipment much, as it was very susceptible to being
destroyed. As to Celerity combat, it honestly made very little
difference. There just aren't enough worthy Celerity-based First
Strike cards.

The only real impact that I saw it have was when we'd loaned just about
all of the group's Backstab cards and the like to one player who liked
the Assamites. We played a lot of combat decks with damage prevention,
so unless you could do unpreventable damage that would get rid of a
minion before they could hit you back, it didn't do you much good.
Luckily for him, Assamites could/can do that quite well.

I can't say what the effect would have been if we'd have played more
S:CE decks. I would think there'd be more of an impact in that case,
as opposed to the combat environment that we played in. Perhaps if
there were more of those types of Celerity-based First Strike cards
there would have been a more noticable difference. Perhaps if we
didn't use as much damage prevention. Hell, perhaps if the Tremere had
Celerity. I'm realizing I haven't been much help. Geh.

p.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <rgskqskd0stai1i05...@4ax.com>, Derek Ray

<lor...@yahoo.com> writes

>>i agree that a dedicated assamite rush deck with psyches, additional
>>strikes etc. can kill a few vampires but they usually end up using most
>>of their resources to oust their prey and then they're finished.
>

>More than 'a few'. You can usually vaporize all your predator's vamps
>and all your prey's vamps. Your next problem is bleeding out your
>vampire-less prey before your grand-predator blows through all three
>of you - the usual difficulty with combat decks.

With a lot of rush decks, that's true. Mostly the IG based ones, simply
because they do it most effectively.

The thing is, I tend to find that, let's say I'm playing a fairly
standard potence/celerity combat deck.

I rush your vampire, I go into combat. I play Torn Signpost. I play
flash, if necessary, to keep it at close range. Play IG, blur. 4
cards, 9 damage (POT CEL). You can't Majesty, and you'd have to play a
Skin of Steel type card (i.e. all damage from a strike, not just
"Prevent 1 damage") to get around it.

Now, were I to be playing Assamites, with a QUI CEL vamp, I rush you
(say, with a Contract, maybe). What options do I have? Well, I *can't*
give myself a good, base strike as with Torn Signpost or Fists of Death.
For each of my strikes I have to play a strike card, or strike for
hands. So, we go into combat, and I want to play some of the Assamite
long range strikes. I play Flash, to go to long (or I could use it to
stay at close, as we assumed with the Brujah above). So, for my strike,
I play Taste of Death. That's 1 blood, doing 1 or 2 aggravated damage.
Now, the POT/CEL crowd were doing three, which is out of the range of
Skin of Rock, but this is still in that range - though if it gets
through, it will send me to torpor. Or I could play Blood Sweat.
Again, 1 blood. This time we have the advantage of not going to torpor.

So, we could play, with our Assamites, assuming a good flow of cards and
play, a rush card (maybe Contract), followed by Flash, followed by Blood
Sweat, Blur, Blood Sweat, Taste of Death. Okay, that's 6 cards to do
only 8 damage, though 2 of that is aggravated. The Brujah managed 9
damage with 5 cards. Also, the Assamites just spent 4 blood. The
Brujah deck has maybe taken one or two hand damage, so it comes off
better blood wise. Your smallest QUI CEL is 5 capacity, and then you go
to 7. Your smallest POT CEL is Jimmy Dunn, at 4, followed by Anvil at
6. Abd al Rashid has to spend 4 blood on that combo, and ends up at 1
blood. Okay, you can play Taste of Vitae - but do you play it midway
through to top yourself back up? At the end? Both? Jimmy only ever
goes down 1 from the Blur. Maybe 1 from a Fists of Death. He goes down
to 2, we'll say. Abd goes down to 1. Okay, so Abd is at long range and
is less likely to take hand damage, so they need something to hit you
with. But what if they *do* hit you with something? Jimmy has a bigger
buffer zone, of 2 blood, to play with.

Also, there is the fact that Abd *is* at long range. You *have* to
supply a source of maneuvers. Jimmy may be able to cruise by without a
maneuver, if the other guy can't maneuver. That 5 card combo - rush,
Torn Signpost, flash, IG, blur - becomes only 4 cards if you *can* drop
the Flash out. Only the Gangrel really have the cards to outpace a
maneuver rich deck (Quick Meld is luvverly), I guess, and a lot of decks
don't seem to bother much with them as defensive maneuvers. But you
*do* need a Flash in the Assamite scenario. If we play on exactly the
same terms as the Assamite deck, not having a pro-active way to stop
Majesty, we drop the IG too. 3 cards - rush, Torn, blur - versus 6
cards - rush, flash, BS, blur, BS, ToD.

Then we come to the fact about Majesty. It's played, a lot. You can't
do much about that fact. Hopefully, to my mind, Sabbat War will contain
ways to make it less attractive, whilst still viable, or less of a no-
brainer. But, in the here and now, we don't have it. So they play
Majesty against your first strike.

The Brujah deck goes Rush - (Flash) - IG. They can't play it.

The Assamite deck goes Rush - Flash - Blood Sweat. They play Majesty.
You play Pysche! and have to go again with the Flash.

You've just wasted a strike and a maneuver on Majesty. And if you don't
play them, you can't do half as much damage. The Assamites don't have
the Auspex for Primal Instincts, but you could try Rapid Thought which
is along the same lines (possibly better, here), so it *can* stop me
wasting cards. But I've already played the maneuver to get me in place,
which is unfortunate.

So, we think about scrapping the maneuver. This is a pity, because two
of the nicest Assamite strikes are Blood Sweat and Taste of Death, both
long range only. So we need close range strikes. For my money, only
the Khabar: Honor cuts it, so we need to have played Contract. But
Contract is only on one vampire. Yes, we save a nice lot of blood,
because it's free, but combat decks do occasionally lose vampires - the
political deck throws a Banishment, maybe, or you do find yourself in a
nasty fight with a deck that just has a little edge in combat, that you
didn't expect. The Brujah deck just rushes with another vampire, and
carries on with a Torn Signpost. The Assamite deck needs the Contract
there, so it plays another one on a new vampire. That's a lot of master
phases going for that. The Brujah deck can play Blood Doll, discipline
cards, Minion Tap, a hunting ground, contest the Elysium, maybe even
have a few Sudden Reversals or Direct Interventions in its hand. Haven
Uncovered *can* be played, but its not a necessity. The Assamite deck,
if it wants to play the Khabar: Honor route, has to have sufficient
Contracts on hand in order to be useful, so that it pulls them as and
when you get new vampires, and it gets new vampires to use them. And if
you're playing the standard rush deck tactics, as we were suggesting in
this thread[0], of killing vampires quickly, your Contract is only going
to be useful for one turn. A Brujah deck has played Blood Doll, useful
over multiple turns, or an Elysium, to scupper the other side, maybe.
You're having to play it simply to set up your combat.

So, then we decide that it isn't the *quantity* of damage that matters,
it's the quality. If we do that, we might just try and put something
useful into the first strike. Unlike the Brujah, we can't pile up a
Torn Signpost, an Increased Strength and an Undead Strength into a 7
damage first (not First) strike. We don't have the ability to add to
damage, so we are more scuppered. And even if we do find some nice
strikes - like Taste of Death, say - we still have problems -
maneuvering, blood cost etc. Since Taste of Death does aggravated
damage, they'll go to torpor. But you can't then play Taste of Vitae
for much, since the first point of damage won't do anything other than
send them to torpor. So you'll regain the point lost in playing Taste
of Death, but won't have the ability to get the point you lose to hand
damage, which a Brujah deck generally can, because of doing multiple
damage.

Then, because Taste of Death only does a small amount of damage, they
hit torpor with most of their blood left. Assamites can't throw an
Amaranth, due to the diablerie restriction, so you'd have to have a
weenie, either in the deck or via Embrace. And you're likely to lose it
in the blood hunt since you're never really likely to have more than 3
votes to hand (Thetmes + Edge), and probably less than that.

Okay, this way you end up with more cards to use, since you're not doing
so much in terms of cards per combat, but you can't burn vampires, and
you *still* can't guarantee the hit. :(

One interesting option does seem to be available, which is the
Fame/Catacombs/Humanitas combination. But you still have the problem of
actually torporising them in the first place. When you start adding
more cards for multiple Fames, Catacombs, Humanitas or whatever, you end
up detracting from the combat. And, to my mind, the Assamites lose out
far more badly from detracting from their combat abilities than the
POT/CEL Brujah-type gang do.

I'd love to see the Assamites do well, but I've never really seen it
possible. Any deck that finds combat a problem can have combat defence,
of the type that will ruin an Assamite deck's day, in spades.

I guess I'll respond to the guys comment that "when was the last time anyone
saw an assamite deck win a tournament?". Well, I felt like I had a shot to
do some damage at DragonCon here this year. I got 4 VPs in three rounds and
would have ended up with 6VPs and a trip to the finals if Mike Perlman had
not played three Anarch Revolts very late in the game to oust me. 4VPs is
not to bad given that the level of play was extremely high at this tourney.
It CAN be done. Easy? Hell no. How? Well read on...

First off before I get to the deck I played at DragonCon, let me direct you
over to some articles I have written in the past on the Assamites. You
REALLY need to read them. Why? I have found that playing the Assamites (at
least for me and I am very biased) is the most challenging clan there is.
The reason is that you almost never can just play the cards in your deck as
they come up. There is a lot of thinking and head games that you have to
play with other Methuselahs. In order to make them successful, you must
fully understand their weaknesses and how to capitalize on their strengths.
This is no different than fully understanding how to play a dedicated
intercept or rush deck. Anyone can pick up one of these decks and play with
them but until you fully understand them, then you will probably not get the
results you are looking for.

Links to the all of the articles can be found at:
http://members.tripod.com/~Lasombra/newsletter.htm

Below is main write-up in the 5th newsletter:
Main Discussion of December: Finding a way to allow combat to gain victory
points
One thing that I continue to notice is that most people playing the
Assamites try to build decks that resemble typical rush combat. Most of
these Methuselahs soon learn that playing a rush style combat deck with the
Assamites generates a lot of destroyed minions around them but rather few
victory points. Why is this?

A successful rush combat deck needs to be deadly in combat while still being
as fast as possible. The Assamites have the first condition easily met with
their combination of celerity and quietus. The second condition is where the
Assamites tend to fall apart. They are simply not fast enough due to them
only having one vampire with the celerity/quietus combination with a
capacity below seven. Over the course of a typical game an Assamite player
averages only a little over three vampires out at any given time. This leads
to the assassins not having enough available rush actions and basic bleeds
for one pool to finish any Methuselah off very quickly. So what can you do?

I have studied most of the Assamite decks that have been posted online and
none of them seem to get around them having insufficient number of actions.
Therefore I believe the key to the Assamites is not to create more actions
but to be as efficient as possible with the actions that they have. It would
be ideal if the Assamites had a way to deal damage to their prey's pool
supply while concentrating on what they do best - combat. Luckily for them
there is a way to do this now without having to wait for the coming
expansion set. The card that makes this possible is Fame.

Fame: Unique Master
Put this card on a ready vampire. If he or she goes into torpor, the
{vampire's controller} burns three pool. Each Methuselah burns one pool
during his or her untap phase if this vampire is in torpor.

The basis of the Fame decks has been around since the Jyhad days but not
until the recent rule changes did it make its way into dedicated combat
decks. Now the famous vampire becomes a target that when hunted down acts
like a bleed for four pool (three for the initial sinking and one during
your prey's untap phase for being in torpor). With just three actions (sink
the famous vampire, rescue and sink again) the Assamites can effectively
bleed for seven pool in a single round and most importantly the pool loss
can not be bounced or reduced. That is impressive for any combat deck.

But what makes Fame work better for the Assamites over the other clans? The
answer comes in the card that defines the essence of the assassins.
Contracts give the Assamites a form of permanent rush combat that is
desperately needed in order to continually punish the hunted vampire. With
just one Contract the famous vampire can no longer quietly escape from harm
due to you not having a single Bum's Rush or Haven Uncovered. Another
advantage that the Assamites have in the Fame style deck is the use if Foul
Blood. If for any reason the famous vampire has to hunt (due to having zero
blood) a well-placed Foul Blood can send the vampire back into torpor and
cost the Methuselah another three pool.

One of the most important things about playing the Fame deck is the
selection of who gets to be hunted. You should take your time in choosing
your victim, as your deck's overall performance will be directly affected by
this decision. I have noticed that in most decks players will include a few
token weenie vampires that help round out their decks. These vampires tend
to show up very early in the game as blockers and such. The token vampires
make good targets due to them being fairly weak and easily sinkable. Another
strategy in choosing the hunted is to find your prey's main vampire that is
blocking other player's actions and make them famous. Selecting the
interceptor will increase your chances of being able to rush into combat via
the Contracts. A third strategy is to pick out your prey's main bleeder and
drop Fame on them. Choosing the heavy bleeder will definitely slow your prey
down because now there are two Methuselahs (you and your grand prey) that
want to see this vampire sent to torpor. This creates a temporary ally in
your grand prey and gives you a chance to oust your prey before he picks up
an additional victory point and six pool. Regardless of the strategy you
choose, the one thing that remains the same with most of the famous vampires
is that they tend to play fairly conservative for the remainder of the game
for fear of being caught. Always keep this in mind and try to use this to
your advantage.

Another aspect to this deck is to consider when is the proper time to play
Fame and rush the vampire. The first thought is to start pounding on your
prey as soon as possible but more times than naught this leads to trouble.
This is because many Methuselahs will slow down or even stop transferring
out additional vampires when they realize what your deck plans to do. This
puts more pressure on your deck to perform and leaves you with even more
pool to burn through for a victory point. About the optimal time to begin
playing Fame and rushing the victim is when your prey transfers down to
around ten to twelve pool. Now your victory point is just a few trips to
torpor away instead of being numerous visits.

Now that you have a grasp on who to make famous and when to rush the last
thing to consider is how do you get them out of torpor so that you can dunk
them again? There are two cards in the game that make this task easier for
the rescuer and they are Humanitas and the Catacombs. Both of the cards give
the rescuer an additional plus one stealth and they burn one less blood if
the action is successful. Both can be stacked on the same vampire to allow
them to rescue the victim at plus two stealth and not have to pay any blood
for the action. One last thing to remember is that when rescuing someone
else's vampire from torpor you do not have to always pay the cost of the
action. Simply announce that you are going to rescue the famous vampire in
torpor and have them pay for your action if it is successful. This is a
fantastic way to keep the hunted low on resources and makes them very
susceptible to a well-aimed Foul Blood.
